analysis.one_liner: Lets federal student loan borrowers refinance their loans at a 4% interest rate.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a House vote; it died in the Education and Workforce Committee when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let people with federal student loans taken out since July 2006 consolidate them into a single loan at a 4% interest rate. Borrowers with higher-rate loans would pay less interest, and the government would cover the cost by giving up interest revenue. The Education and Workforce Committee never acted on it, so it expired when the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal student loan borrowers with loans issued on or after July 1, 2006, who are paying more than 4% interest. They could refinance into a single Direct Consolidation Loan at 4%, lowering their monthly interest costs. Borrowers with loans below 4% would get the lower of their weighted average rate or a small further reduction. Existing borrower benefits — public service loan forgiveness credit, income-based repayment, deferments — would be preserved through the consolidation [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Borrowers with federal loans from July 2006 onward could consolidate into a Federal Direct Consolidation Loan at a 4% interest rate, or a lower rate if their loans' weighted average was already below 4% [S2][S3].

The Department of Education would have to consolidate direct loans and send completed applications to FFEL borrowers within 90 days of enactment, so the relief would happen quickly rather than requiring borrowers to apply from scratch [S2][S3].
The bill protects borrower benefits during consolidation, including credit toward public service loan forgiveness, income-based repayment discharge, deferment, and forbearance [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal government — effectively taxpayers — would take in less interest on tens of millions of refinanced loans, and would use a 0.4% origination fee (added to the loan balance for FFEL consolidations) to cover the cost of making and servicing the loans [S2][S3]. Private lenders holding FFEL loans would lose those loans and the servicing revenue attached to them [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The interest savings would cost the federal government revenue, which either adds to the deficit or must be made up elsewhere [S2].
Borrowers already paying below 4% would see little or no benefit, and FFEL borrowers consolidating would pay a 0.4% origination fee added to their loan balance [S3].

A blanket 4% rate without income limits gives the same break to high earners and low earners alike, which critics of similar refinancing proposals have argued is a poorly targeted use of federal money.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers paying well above 4% — which includes most people with loans from the 2006–2013 era of fixed rates near 6.8% — the savings are real and the bill carefully preserves forgiveness and repayment benefits, so the help would reach the intended people. The main cost is forgone federal interest revenue, and the one-size rate helps higher-income borrowers as much as lower-income ones, making it less targeted than need-based aid. Still, the direct benefit to households is larger and more concrete than the diffuse cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never held a hearing or a vote on it, and it expired when the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Scott Peters introduced the bill on May 25, 2017, joined by 23 cosponsors, all Democrats [S1][S3][S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day; no further action appears in the record for the rest of the Congress [S5].
The bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, without a committee vote or a floor vote [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Borrowers gained nothing because the bill died. The federal budget kept the interest revenue it would have given up, and private lenders holding FFEL loans kept their servicing portfolios rather than losing them to consolidation.

for.name: Rep. Scott Peters
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Federal Student Loan Refinancing Act on May 25, 2017 [S1][S3].

for.name: 23 of 193 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 23 cosponsors were Democrats [S4].

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: Committee of referral; its chair never scheduled a hearing or markup
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on May 25, 2017 and took no recorded action on it for the rest of the Congress [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and all 23 cosponsors were Democrats; with Republican control of the House and the committee, no Republican support appears in the record and the committee never acted on it [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Private lenders and servicers holding FFEL loans
industries.note: The bill would move FFEL loans held by eligible lenders into federal Direct Consolidation Loans, taking those loans and their servicing revenue away from private lenders [S2][S3]. The bill gives lenders' borrowers a 0.25% rate break on consolidation, and consolidating at 4% means borrowers pay less interest than they do on high-rate loans [S3].
The government would forgo interest revenue by refinancing tens of millions of loans at 4%, offset partly by a 0.4% origination fee on FFEL consolidations [S2][S3].
